justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline for the S&P 500 across all three horizons, with the index sitting somewhere in the mid-3500s to low-3600s range. At the one-day horizon, the estimate near 3565 was anchored primarily to the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, with only minimal drift expected given typical daily volatility. For the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 3580, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption consistent with long-run equity risk premium expectations, while acknowledging that a single week offers little meaningful directional signal. At the one-month horizon, the estimate of 3610 incorporates a slightly larger expected return, consistent with historical monthly equity performance, but the range widens considerably to reflect the compounding of uncertainty over a longer window.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated primarily to historical realized volatility of the S&P 500. At the daily level, the roughly 95-point half-width on each side reflects annualized volatility of around 18–20%, which is consistent with the environment at the time. As the horizon extends to one week and then one month, the intervals widen in proportion to the square root of time, following standard statistical assumptions about return distributions. The one-month interval spanning roughly 820 points (3200 to 4020) reflects both this time-scaling and an added fat-tail allowance, since monthly returns exhibit more skew and kurtosis than a simple normal model would suggest.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals entirely. On the downside, a sharp escalation in Federal Reserve tightening signals, a significant credit event, or a geopolitical shock could easily drive the index below 3200 within a month. Systemic financial stress — such as contagion from a major institutional failure — represents a tail risk that is difficult to price precisely but has historically produced moves far exceeding normal volatility bands. On the upside, a surprise dovish pivot from the Fed, a stronger-than-expected earnings season, or a sudden de-escalation in macro uncertainty could push prices above 4020 more quickly than the baseline anticipates. These scenarios are not captured well by symmetric interval construction, and in practice the downside tail risk was likely larger than the upside tail at the time.
